title: Design an Image Copyright Detection System
prompt:
A content library imports images from external stock-photo providers. Today, human reviewers accept or reject each image, and their decisions are recorded in a data warehouse. Design an automated copyright-review stage that can accept an image, reject it, or send an uncertain case to a human reviewer.

Explain how you would sample and label training and evaluation data, choose metrics and thresholds, decide whether a new model should replace the current one, and measure business impact. Include the prediction service and the feedback loop from review outcomes to training.

Extend the system to video: sampling roughly one frame every ten seconds increases the image workload by about 50 times. How would you evaluate video-level decisions and handle the additional workload?

response.placeholder: Describe the review decisions, data flow, evaluation, rollout, and video extension.
response.reference_answer:
## Review workflow and decision contract

The ingestion path starts with external stock-photo providers. Human reviewers currently accept or reject images; their decisions flow to a data warehouse. Add an automatic review service ahead of that queue: accept sufficiently confident compliant images, reject sufficiently confident violations, and route uncertain cases to reviewers. Keep provider, image, model, policy, and review identifiers so each outcome is auditable. Clarify what copyright evidence and labels are available before choosing a model; visual similarity alone does not determine rights.

## Sampling, labels, and evaluation

Build training data from reviewed images and warehouse decisions, accounting for reviewer disagreement, policy changes, class imbalance, and provider differences. Audit samples from every automatic decision branch so rejected and accepted items do not disappear from the labeling loop. Use a held-out temporal split and keep near-duplicate image families together. Report precision and recall for violations, calibration, false acceptance and false rejection costs, review coverage, and slices by provider and content type.

Choose acceptance and rejection thresholds according to those costs and reviewer capacity. Compare a candidate with the incumbent on the same held-out data and current traffic. A gain in aggregate accuracy is insufficient if costly violations or a provider slice regress.

## Serving, feedback, and deployment

Prediction servers load a versioned model and return a score and decision to ingestion. Reviewer outcomes and sampled audits are written back to the warehouse, then used in a controlled training and evaluation loop. Keep candidate evaluation separate from training selection. Shadow a new model, then canary it with guardrails for error costs, review queue delay, prediction latency, and review effort. Preserve a rollback path to the incumbent.

Business impact includes review effort saved, time to accept usable content, rejection errors, and the cost of missed violations. Measure impact at comparable incoming volume and quality; reducing human review alone is not success.

## Video extension

The stated sampling interval yields approximately fifty times the image workload. Plan capacity, queue isolation, batching, caching and duplicate-frame suppression before admitting the extra volume. Frame samples from a video are correlated, so split and evaluate at video level. Define how frame evidence becomes a video decision and validate that policy on labeled videos. More selective sampling may reduce cost but can miss brief violations; compare that trade-off against the fixed-interval baseline.

## Follow-up discussion

What happens when a provider or policy changes? How would you label uncertain cases consistently? How do you estimate missed violations among auto-accepted items? When does additional automation increase risk or reviewer workload?
